AI has a problem. Specifically, modern generative-AI-based chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude have a problem. Not a technical problem. In fact, they work much better than most of their critics realize, and they’re improving at an alarming rate.

The problem is that people don’t like them. Some people do. Others use them despite misgivings. A lot of people really hate them. For a while, this was simply the way that it was: another topic for us all to get polarized over, but we could mostly live and let live.

That’s now starting to change.

In a recent essay , I made the claim that if you write safety-critical code, it is no longer responsible to do so without AI assistance. That is because AI can spot bugs—possibly exploitable bugs—that people can’t. Writing code with some security aspect, say user management, without any AI review as part of your process, more or less guarantees that your users will be increasingly vulnerable to attack.

If you dislike modern AI—and I dislike many aspects of it myself—but you concede the above point, then this puts us in a very unpleasant position. We now have a tool that is absolutely crucial and at the same time morally objectionable to many people.

This raises a natural question. Can AI be fixed? Can we build the same thing that we have now, with the power to do some of the things we now need it to do—like code review—but without the objectionable parts. And, while we’re at it, what exactly are all the objectionable parts?

This is really a two-part question. Take, for example, the destruction of rare books that some AI companies are now engaged in. They are doing this simply to create a private repository of data that many others have already created for themselves. This is something that is technically utterly unnecessary. For one thing, the data already exists several times over, and for another, Google (the first to do it) have shown that the scanning can be done non-destructively. So technically, yes, we can absolutely build AI without destroying books.

That’s an interesting conclusion, but not a very practical one, since the current system is still set up so that destructive book scanning is the move these companies feel forced to make. We can do it without, but we aren’t doing it without. So we must also ask a follow-up question. Is there a realistic scenario in which some entity does actually build AI the ethical way?

To make things concrete, let’s focus on the motivating example: AI that can do a natural language code review and catch security bugs that a human reviewer misses. What’s more, if we’re going to be realistic, we will need to assume that our attacker has no qualms about using unethically built AI. If Claude or ChatGPT are substantially better at spotting security bugs than an ethically built AI, we still have a problem .

That is the plan: to go through all the things that people object to in modern AI, as she is practiced today, and to see to what extent each is inherent to the technology— required to make it work—or simply an artifact of the hyper-capitalist race to the cliff edge that we find ourselves engaged in.

In my naïveté, I briefly thought of this as a single blog post, but it is of course a bigger project than that. In this first part, we will focus on the issue of using copyrighted data to train LLMs without consent, and save other issues for future posts.

For a large part, the title question of this post is a research question . For many problematic practices, we simply don’t know whether we can build it without them, and we need to investigate. Some parts are easy, others more difficult. The most likely conclusion of this series (assuming I finish it) is that it’s worth trying . Even if we cannot fully eliminate all the problems, we can eliminate a lot of them, and we can keep studying the rest. Very few things we do are entirely unproblematic. Eating or having children or moving from A to B come with plenty of impact on the world around us. We study these impacts, and we fix them where we can. Where we can’t, we either use technology cautiously or not at all. I see no reason to treat AI any differently.

For this reason, I will flag concrete research questions with RQ where they come up. I think this will paint a fairly clean research program for the near future.

So, on to the question of this particular post: can we train an AI that can do code review as well as Claude, using no “stolen data”?

## Is it stolen?

Ethics and legality are two different things. Something can be legal but not ethical, or vice versa. Still, in a functioning society, they should be at least somewhat aligned, so it’s worth asking first whether AI training data legally counts as “stolen”.

AI models are trained on data taken from the internet. This goes all the way back to the first GPT in 2018, which was trained on books that were free to read , but not openly licensed beyond that. The authors did not give permission for the work to be re-used in any way the downloader likes, only for it to be read.

This is true for a lot of content on the internet. You’re allowed to read it, but you’re not allowed to, say, copy it and put it on your own website. That’s the problem at hand. No permission was given explicitly to train an AI model on the data.

To give the counter-point: some people argue that what an AI model is doing when consumes the data during training is reading. It goes over the data, learns from it, memorizes some of it, or memorizes general trends and themes. It’s exactly what people do when they read.

If you take this point of view, nothing is “stolen”: what companies do is a kind of scaled-up reading. You might say that reading at such a scale should not be legally protected, but it’s a new phenomenon so it’s not clear in what way the law applies.

It’s worth being precise about which things are legally contentious. If you produce content and put it online for people to read, there are limits to what you can forbid people from doing. The main actions that copyright allows you to control are copying, republishing and creating derivative works. This raises two very separate questions that people don’t often clearly separate.

First, is the AI model itself a derivative work, and second, is the output of an AI model a derivative work?

Consider GPT. The model itself is a file on a harddrive, containing probably a terabyte or so of floating-point numbers arranged in matrices. These numbers were derived from a lot of copyrighted data, and much of the data can probably be retrieved from them verbatim.

If we consider this file a derivative work, then OpenAI might defend themselves by saying that they aren’t publishing any derivative work. They never show anybody their model, so they’re not publishing anything. A clear precedent here is the way a search engine works: it crawls the world wide web, downloads all of it, and keeps a local copy in a kind of format that allows for keyword search. This is a local copy of copyrighted data, and multinational companies have been built on it.

In Europe, collecting a bunch of copyrighted data in a local database is not allowed by itself: the reason why you’re doing it matters. The reason search engine operator can still do this is because an exception is made for certain uses.

In the US, there is a fair use doctrine that allows a variety of uses of copyrighted material without the consent of the copyright holder. Various arguments can be used to argue fair use: non-commercial activity, small scale or personal use and so on. The argument for AI (and search engines) is that the use of the data is transformative . A search engine indexing a book changes the nature and use of the data in such a way, or so the argument goes, that the original copyright no longer applies.

This is how search engine indices are justified, and how companies are attempting to justify the training of AI models. In US-style jurisdictions, the attempted justification is fair use. In European-style jurisdictions, it is in principle not allowed, but it is common for carve-outs to be created for emerging technologies.

This shows how important our question—whether AI can be fixed—really is. If we cannot build AI without this kind of copyright infringement, and we agree that we need AI, then we find ourselves exactly where we were at the start of the world wide web: we need a carve-out or we can’t have the technology. Or more realistically, we need a carve-out or we are forced to rely on US companies.

If, however, AI can be built ethically, without copyright infringement, then we don’t need a carve out, and indeed, we can require US companies to train models without copyright infringement if they want to deploy them in Europe. The central question is whether the copyrighted data is a key ingredient. We need to know that before we can make an informed decision on what the law should look like.

The picture changes when we look at the output of AI models. Not too long ago, you could ask ChatGPT for the lyrics to Don’t Cry for Me Argentina , and it would produce them faithfully. This is a clear, unauthorized, public republishing of copyrighted data. Moreover, it still occurs if we allow the collection and use of the training data. If you claim fair use—or if Europe introduces an exception for AI training—then OpenAI still commits the copyright violation at the moment their model produces the lyrics and sends them to me.

In short, a company that can legally train an AI on copyrighted data, may still be liable if the model decides to spit out verbatim copies of that data when it’s hosting the model. Given the shaky reliability of AI guardrails at the moment, this should cause AI companies some headaches.

All of this is useful to understand, but it glosses over perhaps the most important issue. We’re looking here at the anger that people have for AI practices, and that goes beyond legal technicalities. People placed their content on the internet in good faith for a certain kind of use, and that content was then scraped at scale and re-used at an entirely different scale than people imagined.

That’s the ethical question . If it is legal to do all this, that’s mostly because the technology didn’t yet exist when the law was established. We’re still figuring out what the law says about search engines exactly. If it’s legal, it’s because of a technicality.

The question of this post is whether we can build AI without that sense of betrayal, regardless of its legal status. For this part of the series: can we build AI using only data that was freely and gladly given for any use?

A very clear starting point here is the Common Pile : a collection of almost every source of text content on the web that is either in the public domain or under a permissive license, (usually some form of Creative Commons). It includes:

- All Wikimedia projects. Wikipedia, Wikibooks, Wiktionary, etc. Not just their content, but also their talk pages and community pages.

- All StackExchange content.
